content: Individuals with sickle cell disease are highly vulnerable to pneumococcal infections, which can be life-threatening. Infants, particularly those under 23 months of age, are at an especially elevated risk. However, traditional polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccines have shown limited effectiveness in this age group. Recently developed conjugate pneumococcal vaccines may offer a promising alternative to reduce the incidence of these infections in individuals with sickle cell disease. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of pneumococcal vaccines in reducing both morbidity and mortality among people with sickle cell disease. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches, manual searches of relevant journals, and conference proceedings. Additionally, pharmaceutical companies and field experts were contacted for further information. The most recent search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register was conducted on December 9, 2011. The review included all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared different pneumococcal vaccine regimens—either polysaccharide or conjugate vaccines—or compared vaccination to no vaccination in individuals with sickle cell disease. Two independent reviewers selected the studies, extracted the data, and assessed the quality of the trials. Out of nine identified trials, five trials involving a total of 547 participants met the inclusion criteria. Among these, only one trial reported the incidence of pneumococcal infections. This trial found that the polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccine (PPV14) did not significantly reduce the risk of infection in children under three years of age. However, the vaccine was associated with only minor adverse effects. Three trials investigating conjugate pneumococcal vaccines demonstrated enhanced antibody responses compared to control groups, including in infants. However, these trials did not measure clinical outcomes. Conjugate pneumococcal vaccines have previously been shown to be safe and effective in healthy individuals, including those under two years of age. The controlled trials included in this review confirmed the immunogenicity of these vaccines in individuals with sickle cell disease, meaning they successfully stimulated an immune response. Observational studies in this population further support these findings. Based on this evidence, the authors recommend the use of conjugate pneumococcal vaccines in individuals with sickle cell disease. Future randomized trials in this population are necessary to determine the most effective vaccination regimen, particularly as newer and potentially more effective vaccines become available. These trials should focus on measuring clinical outcomes to assess vaccine effectiveness. The trials included in this review were conducted between 1983 and 2003, and no additional relevant trials were identified up to December 2011. As a result, the authors do not plan to update this review until new trials are published.
